claims.text: The initial high-entropy alloy is a homogeneous single-phase solid solution.
The initial alloy exhibits ductile behavior under standard conditions.
High-stress demanding-service conditions induce nanoscale segregation or an incipient phase transformation in the nominally single-phase alloy.
Stress-induced nanoscale segregation localizes compositional fluctuations.
Localized segregated regions are preferential sites for crack initiation.
Crack initiation at segregated regions reduces overall toughness and promotes brittle fracture.
Controlled processing or compositional variations can promote the early onset of nanoscale segregation.
Nanoscale compositional fluctuations or incipient secondary phases create localized regions of embrittlement.
Stress and thermal activation enhance diffusion or destabilize the uniform solid solution.
Enhanced diffusion or solid-solution destabilization leads to segregated regions.
Segregated regions nucleate microcracks and lower the effective fracture energy.
Microcrack nucleation and reduced fracture energy cause a transition from ductile to brittle fracture.
Specimens exhibiting induced nanoscale segregation will have lower toughness than the baseline single-phase alloy.
Phase separation or chemical segregation will be observable along crack paths in the modified specimens.
The baseline alloy has no detectable segregation and exhibits robust toughness and ductile fracture under standard or moderate service conditions.
The embrittlement effect emerges only when mechanical stress exceeds a threshold intensity, potentially assisted by temperature or cyclic loading.
Below the proposed threshold, the alloy retains its ductile single-phase character.
The onset threshold and toughness reduction depend on alloying elements and processing history.

contradictions.description: The central hypothesis attributes segregation to mechanical stress, but the modified samples are deliberately processed or compositionally changed to promote segregation before or apart from loading. This design can conflate processing-induced segregation with stress-induced segregation.

The samples are described as coming from the same HEA batch while compositional adjustment is also proposed as an intervention; compositionally adjusted specimens would not strictly represent the same batch or alloy composition.
